vulnerabilities.title: RWX_SHELLCODE_EXECUTION

root_cause.description: The program allocates an anonymous mmap page with PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC (protection=7, flags=MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS=0x22), reads up to 0xfff bytes of unvalidated attacker-controlled data from stdin directly into this RWX page via read(0, mmap_buf, 0xfff), and then transfers control to it via 'call rax' where rax holds the mmap base address. No validation, sanitization, or integrity check is performed on the input bytes before execution. The bytes are treated as executable machine code with no restrictions on instruction content. This is a deliberate shellcode execution challenge design: the mmap RWX allocation (prot=7) combined with unvalidated stdin read and direct indirect call constitutes the root cause — attacker-controlled data flows directly into executable memory and is invoked as code.

affected_objects: mmap'd RWX anonymous page (0x1000 bytes, prot=7, flags=0x22)

data_flow: main calls init() at 0x13f3 which installs seccomp filter (setup_seccomp) and sets alarm(60)
main allocates RWX page: mmap(NULL, 0x1000, PROT_RWX(7), MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANON(0x22), -1, 0) at 0x141b, result stored in [rbp-0x10]
mmap return checked against MAP_FAILED (-1) at 0x1424; if MAP_FAILED -> _abort('mmap failed!')
main reads stdin into RWX page: read(0, [rbp-0x10], 0xfff) at 0x144c, size = [rbp-0x4](0x1000) - 1 = 0xfff
read return checked: test rax,rax at 0x1451; if zero -> _abort('read failed!') — only rejects zero-byte reads, does not validate content
main executes user input: mov rax,[rbp-0x10]; call rax at 0x1462/0x1466 — direct transfer of control to attacker-controlled bytes in RWX page

security_check.expected: Input data read into executable memory should be validated, sandboxed, or restricted to a known-safe instruction set before execution. At minimum, the execution context should prevent arbitrary syscall invocation.
security_check.actual: No validation of input bytes is performed. The only checks are: (1) mmap return != MAP_FAILED (allocation success), (2) read return != 0 (some bytes received). Neither check constrains the content of the bytes. A seccomp filter (installed in init() before the read) constrains syscalls available to the executed shellcode but does not prevent code execution itself.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: No input validation on shellcode content. No restriction on which instructions can be executed. The seccomp filter is the sole mitigation constraining the shellcode's syscall capabilities, but it does not prevent the execution of arbitrary code — it only limits what syscalls the code can invoke.

vulnerable_operation.operation: EXEC (indirect call to attacker-controlled RWX memory)
vulnerable_operation.expression: call rax  (where rax = [rbp-0x10] = mmap(NULL, 0x1000, 7, 0x22, -1, 0) base, filled by read(0, rax, 0xfff))
vulnerable_operation.target: RWX anonymous mmap page containing attacker-supplied bytes from stdin
vulnerable_operation.size: up to 0xfff (4095) bytes of executable code

impact.reason: Attacker-controlled code executing in process context can perform arbitrary memory reads/writes within the process address space (subject to seccomp syscall constraints). The shellcode runs with full process privileges and can access any mapped memory region. The seccomp filter blocks write(1) and restricts read to fd==4, but does not prevent memory access via direct load/store instructions.

If the attacker supplies non-executable or invalid byte sequences (e.g., 'AAAA' as observed in S1 probe_io), the CPU will attempt to decode and execute them as instructions, leading to SIGSEGV or other illegal instruction faults. This was confirmed by S1 runtime probe (F016: input 'AAAA' resulted in Segmentation fault).

evidence.description: mmap is called with prot=7 (PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE|PROT_EXEC) and flags=0x22 (MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS) at 0x140e (edx=7) and 0x1409 (ecx=0x22). This creates a Read-Write-Execute anonymous page — the most permissive memory protection, allowing the page to be written to and then executed.

read(0, mmap_buf, 0xfff) at 0x144c reads up to 0xfff bytes from stdin (fd=0) directly into the RWX mmap page. The size is computed as [rbp-0x4](0x1000) - 1 = 0xfff via 'mov eax,[rbp-0x4]; sub eax,1; movsxd rdx,eax' at 0x1437-0x143d. No content validation is performed on the read data.

Direct execution of user input: 'mov rax,QWORD PTR [rbp-0x10]; call rax' at 0x1462/0x1466. rax holds the mmap base address which now contains attacker-controlled bytes from stdin. This is an unconditional indirect call to attacker-controlled executable memory.

read() return value check is incomplete: 'test rax,rax; jne 0x1462' at 0x1451/0x1454 only branches to execution if read returned non-zero. This rejects zero-byte reads (EOF) but does not check for negative return values (error) — though more critically, it does not validate the content of bytes read, only that some bytes were received.

init() is called at 0x13f3 (main+0x14) BEFORE mmap and read. init() calls setup_seccomp() at 0x13d7 which installs the seccomp filter via seccomp_load(). This confirms seccomp is active during shellcode execution — the filter constrains syscalls but does not prevent code execution itself.

Seccomp whitelist: seccomp_init(0)=SCMP_ACT_KILL default deny. Allowed syscalls: open(2), openat(257), read(0) with arg0==4 filter (SCMP_CMP_EQ,4), mmap(9), fstat(5), brk(12), exit(60), exit_group(231). write(1) is NOT allowed. read from fd 0 is NOT allowed (only fd==4). This is the sole mitigation constraining shellcode capabilities — it limits syscalls but does not prevent arbitrary code execution in userspace.

The complete data flow chain: stdin -> read(0, RWX_page, 0xfff) -> no validation -> call rax (execute). Combined with RWX mmap (E001) and no content check (E002/E004), this constitutes arbitrary code execution by design. The seccomp filter (E006) is the only constraint on what the executed code can do at the syscall level.

verification_required: Confirm seccomp filter is correctly installed and active during shellcode execution (S1 resolved U002: init() called before read, seccomp active)
Confirm that the seccomp filter cannot be bypassed (e.g., via x32 ABI, seccomp architecture mismatch, or filter ordering issues)
Confirm whether the read(fd==4) argument filter can be satisfied by shellcode (e.g., open two files to reach fd 4, or use dup/dup2 if not blocked — note dup/dup2 are NOT in whitelist)
Determine if there are alternative exfiltration channels given write(1) is blocked (e.g., mmap-based, timing side-channel, or other creative approaches) — this is S3/S4 scope

non_vulnerabilities.description: Seccomp filter installation logic: seccomp_init(0) with SCMP_ACT_KILL default, accumulates rule_add return codes via OR into [rbp-0xc], checks accumulated error after seccomp_load, exits(1) if any rule failed.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The seccomp setup correctly checks return codes from seccomp_init, seccomp_rule_add, and seccomp_load. The error accumulation via OR and final check at 0x1329 (cmp [rbp-0xc],0; je ok; exit(1)) is sound — if any rule_add or seccomp_load fails, the process exits. The filter itself is the security mechanism, not a vulnerability. The filter's constraints (blocking write, restricting read to fd==4) are intentional design choices for the challenge.

non_vulnerabilities.description: mmap return value check: cmp [rbp-0x10], -1 (MAP_FAILED) at 0x1424; jne to continue; else _abort('mmap failed!').
non_vulnerabilities.reason: The MAP_FAILED check is correct and follows standard practice. If mmap fails, the program aborts rather than proceeding to read into an invalid pointer. This is a proper error handling path, not a vulnerability.

non_vulnerabilities.description: setvbuf calls on stdin/stdout/stderr with _IONBF(2), alarm(60), then setup_seccomp().
non_vulnerabilities.reason: setvbuf with _IONBF disables buffering (standard CTF practice for reliable I/O). alarm(60) sets a 60-second timeout (standard anti-hang measure). These are configuration choices, not vulnerabilities. The ordering (seccomp installed before mmap/read in main) is correct.

Simple error reporting function. Uses printf with '%s' format string and a caller-provided message pointer — no format string vulnerability since the format is a literal '%s' string at .rodata, not user-controlled. The msg argument is always a string literal from the caller (main), not attacker-controlled.

non_vulnerabilities.description: libseccomp.so.2 is a NEEDED library with no RPATH/RUNPATH in the binary, resolved from system path /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: As S1 noted (risk LOW), LD_LIBRARY_PATH would take priority over the system path if set, potentially allowing library substitution. However, this is a standard runtime fact of dynamic linking on Linux, not a binary vulnerability. In a normal execution environment (no attacker-controlled LD_LIBRARY_PATH), the library resolves correctly. This is not a vulnerability in the binary itself.

unresolved.description: Whether the seccomp filter has any bypass (e.g., x32 ABI syscall numbers with 0x40000000 prefix, architecture-specific filter gaps, or seccomp filter ordering issues)
unresolved.reason: S2 performs static semantic analysis only. Seccomp bypass analysis requires dynamic verification (testing specific syscall numbers against the installed filter at runtime), which is S3's scope.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 should dynamically test whether the seccomp filter can be bypassed via alternative syscall conventions or architecture mismatches.

unresolved.description: Whether the read(fd==4) constraint can be practically satisfied by shellcode to achieve file exfiltration
unresolved.reason: The seccomp filter allows open/openat (which would return fd 3 for the first open, fd 4 for the second). dup/dup2 are NOT in the whitelist. Shellcode would need to open two files (or open one file twice) to reach fd 4 for read. Whether this is achievable and whether data can be exfiltrated without write(1) is an exploitation strategy question.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3/S4 to determine the practical exploitation strategy given the seccomp constraints — this is beyond S2's vulnerability analysis scope.

unresolved.description: Exact runtime base address of the mmap'd RWX page
unresolved.reason: PIE + mmap ASLR randomize the base address. The address is only known at runtime. This affects exploitation strategy (shellcode needs to be position-independent or use relative addressing), not the vulnerability itself.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3/S4 to handle ASLR in exploitation strategy. The vulnerability (arbitrary code execution) exists regardless of the specific runtime address.
